z-m-11-01.title: Table total bigger than number of students. Table wrong?
z-m-11-01.topic: Table totals and surveyed people count (data where one person marked multiple)
z-m-11-01.goal: When table total differs from survey count, don't call wrong immediately. State needed info like survey method and revise judgment as new details come.
z-m-11-01.material:
Grade 4 Class 3 has 28 students. Dem survey desired field-trip place; table counts students marking ○ for each place.
Place: Museum 12, Zoo 10, Science center 9, Amusement park 7, Total 38.
Jia say, "Total 38 but class get 28 students. Table wrong!" Table written in words only. Rows are place and number of students. 3 4 28 12 10 9 7 38 38 28
z-m-11-01.thinking.0: Separating what table alone can/can't say
z-m-11-01.prereq.0: Reading table item counts and adding (Grades 3-4) 3 4
z-m-11-01.prereq.1: Survey can ask one choice or several choices
z-m-11-01.s.s1.prompt: Data reveal piece by piece; choose your thought each time.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.hint.0: Put total and student count side by side; first inspect difference.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.hint.1: Use small example 3 students to count extra marks if one marks two places. 3
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Now known only table and 28 students; survey form unseen. 28
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.after: Total 38 could come from survey method or double counting. Need see survey sheets to know. 38
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Total differ from students, so counting wrong
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You blame counting only because total differs. Could survey method cause this?
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Until see survey sheet, can't decide table wrong
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You stop at right place; same table total fit differ by survey method.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: If total exceeds people, table always correct
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You believe too quickly. High total fit be counting error too; must check.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Survey form said mark places you want, up to two. Teacher sorting forms first said all 28 students marked at least one place. 28
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: How many students marked two places?
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.after: If all marked at least one and at most two, total 38 marks=28 students + number choosing second place. So 10 chose two. 38 28 10
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You correctly see 38−28 gives extra marks, equal to people who marked one extra time. 28 38
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You maybe take half of 28. Think meaning of gap between 38 marks and 28 people. 28 38 28
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You maybe halve 38. Count extra marks when one person picks two places. 38
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Teacher rechecked from start; earlier assumption wrong. 4 students marked no places; other 24 marked one or two. 4 24
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now how many marked two places?
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.after: Among 24, if 10 chose one and 14 chose two, marks=10+28=38. New info changes answer though table same. 24 10 14 10 28 38
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You confuse people who marked none with people who marked two. Different people.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You carry earlier answer forward unchanged. Check whether newly learned 4 belong in calculation. 4
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You recalculate using new info. 24 people choose one/two and produce 38 marks. 24 38
z-m-11-01.s.s1.reflect: At first were you closer to 'table wrong' or 'can't tell'? How did survey form and 4 nonresponders change each? What remains unknown? 4
z-m-11-01.s.s2.prompt: Knowing form says up to two choices, choose all safe statements from table and form.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine one student marked museum and zoo. Which boxes count them?
z-m-11-01.s.s2.hint.1: For each statement, check whether same student could be counted twice.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.o.a: People choosing museum or zoo total 22 22
z-m-11-01.s.s2.r.a: 12+10=22 might count same person twice. Say 22 or fewer, not exactly 22. 12 10 22 22 22
z-m-11-01.s.s2.r.b: Each cell counts people who marked that place, so safe to read.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.o.c: 38, sum of four table counts, is number of students who marked ○ 38
z-m-11-01.s.s2.r.c: 38 counts marks, not people; one may mark twice. 38
z-m-11-01.s.s2.o.d: 12 museum choosers and 10 zoo choosers are different people 12 10
z-m-11-01.s.s2.r.d: You could choose two, so same person may belong to both.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.o.e: Science center choosers 2 more than amusement park choosers 2
z-m-11-01.s.s2.r.e: Each cell counts choosers for that place, so comparing two cells safe.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.explain: One cell value counts people choosing that place, so reading/comparing single cells safe. Sum can count same person multiple times, not total unique people.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.prompt: Jia says total bigger than students means table wrong. What say, and what else need to decide if wrong?
z-m-11-01.s.s3.hint.0: Think what survey method would make table total equal people count.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.hint.1: Give one possible reason total high and what check would verify it.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Even if total high, I need know ...
z-m-11-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You avoid deciding wrong and give a case where total can exceed?
z-m-11-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You state specifically what else needed?
z-m-11-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Your response sound collaborative, no scold Jia?
z-m-11-01.s.s3.model.0: High total doesn't prove error. If each can mark two or more, total may exceed people. Check survey sheet for number choices allowed.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.model.1: We don't know yet if table wrong. Other class students may answer, or same student counted twice; check who responded and counting method.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: You also suggest checking response group and counting method, besides multiple answers.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.model.2: Jia wrong; table correct. Multiple choices make total exceed people, so check form.

z-m-11-02.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in a solution
z-m-11-02.title: Minseo pictograph reading: what looks odd?
z-m-11-02.topic: What large/small pictures represent in pictograph
z-m-11-02.goal: Counterexample shows counting pictures only can mislead when picture sizes differ; state conditions where picture count comparison okay.
z-m-11-02.material:
Daily bread sales at four local bakeries shown in pictograph. Big bread icon means 10 loaves; small icon means 1. No image, so table written in words.
Bakery | Big icons | Small icons
가 | 3 | 4
나 | 2 | 9
다 | 4 | 0
라 | 3 | 7
Minseo read graph and wrote 6 summary lines. 10 1 3 4 2 9 4 0 3 7
z-m-11-02.prereq.0: Reading values of big/small icons as tens/ones (Grade 3 pictograph) 3
z-m-11-02.s.s1.prompt: Which line of Minseo summary odd? (Line numbers start 1.) 1
z-m-11-02.s.s1.hint.0: To check line 6, find sales at bakery with most icons and fewest, compare. 6
z-m-11-02.s.s1.hint.1: Put sales numbers from lines 2-4 in order and compare line 6 conclusion. 2 4 6
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.0: 1. Big bread picture means 10, small means 1. 1 10 1
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.1: 2. Bakery 가 has 3 big and 4 small: 30+4=34. 2 3 4 30 4 34
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.2: 3. Bakery 나 has 2 big and 9 small: 20+9=29. 3 2 9 20 9 29
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.3: 4. Bakery 다 only 4 big: 40. 라 has 3 big and 7 small: 37. 4 4 40 3 7 37
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.4: 5. Picture counts: 가 7, 나 11, 다 4, 라 10. 5 7 11 4 10
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.5: 6. Most icons at 나 (11), so 나 sold most. 6 11
z-m-11-02.s.s1.explain: Line 6 odd. Different-size icons represent different quantities, so more icons no mean more sales. 나 has 11 but sold 29; 다 has 4 big icons and sold 40, most. 6 11 29 4 40
z-m-11-02.s.s2.prompt: In this graph, counting icons might be wrong. Choose cases where icon-count alone tells which side has more.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.hint.0: Compare bakery 가 (big3, small4) and 나 (big2, small9), comparing big/small counts separately. 3 4 2 9
z-m-11-02.s.s2.hint.1: For each choice, make example and test whether side with more icons must also sell more.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.o.a: Both bakeries use only big icons
z-m-11-02.s.s2.r.a: With one icon size, each stands for same amount, so icon count comparison works.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.o.b: Icon count difference huge, like 11 vs 4 11 4
z-m-11-02.s.s2.r.b: You think big gap safe. But graph's 나 vs 다 flips despite gap.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.o.c: One bakery has more big and more small icons than other
z-m-11-02.s.s2.r.c: You find if one has more of both sizes, total must be larger.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.r.d: Mix alone not enough. Compare counts separately by size.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.explain: If one icon size only, or one side has more big and more small icons, icon count comparison works. If sizes mixed and one has more big but other more small, calculate values.
z-m-11-02.s.s3.prompt: Use numbers explain why line 6 wrong for this graph. Write icon counts and sales for two bakeries. 6
z-m-11-02.s.s3.hint.0: Find icon count and sales for bakery 다 and 나, write two lines.
z-m-11-02.s.s3.hint.1: First sentence compare which bakery has more/fewer icons versus more/fewer sales.
z-m-11-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Bakery 나 has ... icons but ...
z-m-11-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You calculate to ensure both icon count and sales match?
z-m-11-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You explain more icons≠more sales because icons represent different values?
z-m-11-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If you add a case where icon count comparison works, check it really does?
z-m-11-02.s.s3.model.0: 나 has most icons, 11, but only 2 are big, so 20+9=29. 다 has only 4 icons, all big, so 40. Icon sizes represent different quantities, so don't just count pictures. 11 2 20 9 29 4 40
z-m-11-02.s.s3.model.1: Big icon=10, small=1, so multiply big count by 10 and small by 1, not total icons. 가=34, 라=37; icon counts 7 and 10, same order but difference changes. 10 1 10 1 34 37 7 10
z-m-11-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: It also gives example where order stays same, separating it from accidental correctness.

z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Wetin you fit talk from dis result?
z-m-11-04.title: Why results different between raising hands and secret paper vote?
z-m-11-04.topic: How survey method (raise hands, paper vote) affect result
z-m-11-04.goal: Use data check say with same class, different survey method fit give different result, and revise wetin you fit talk and how sure you fit be each time new data come.
z-m-11-04.material: Class 2 of Grade 4 get 24 students. Dem wan decide game to play together for break. Options na dodgeball, board games and skipping rope, and each person vote for only one. Half of 24 na 12.
z-m-11-04.thinking.0: Compare two sets of data from different methods
z-m-11-04.thinking.1: Adjust range of wetin you say when new data come
z-m-11-04.thinking.2: Write sentence wey report result with its conditions
z-m-11-04.prereq.0: Read vote results in table and find total
z-m-11-04.prereq.1: Know half of whole (half of 24 na 12)
z-m-11-04.s.s1.prompt: Vote results dey show step by step. Each step, choose wetin you fit talk.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.hint.0: Put numbers for dodgeball, board games and skipping rope for two votes side by side, and compare each with 12 (half).
z-m-11-04.s.s1.hint.1: Look separately whether order (who first) same and whether size (how many people) same.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.info: First day, everybody keep eyes open and raise hand for one choice. Results na dodgeball 14, board games 6 and skipping rope 4 (24 total). Wen dem raise hands, other friends fit see each other raise hands.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.after: You must tell apart fact inside this vote (14) from guess about students' real feelings. Both kinds of statements fit this step.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Students wey choose dodgeball by raising hand na 14, more than 12, so you fit say for this vote e more than half
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You report the vote result as e be and add range 'for this vote'.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: You no fit trust raising-hands method, so nothing fit be said from this result
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Even if method get weakness, na data wey all 24 people join. Throwing am away as nothing too much.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Dem fit see each other, so some students fit raise hand to follow others, so we need check more whether dodgeball really popular
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You think about fact say method fit affect result, then adjust how sure you be.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Next day, dem vote again with unnamed slips. Results na dodgeball 10, board games 8 and skipping rope 6 (24 total).
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: How we suppose say 'dodgeball get most' and 'more than half choose dodgeball'?
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Dodgeball get most both times. But whether e pass half (12) change with method. How sure you fit be depend on 'wetin' you talk.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Both statements fit talk as dem be. First-day vote more reliable because same number of people
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: 24 people vote both times. Same number of people no be reason to say first day more reliable.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 'Get most' fit be said for both times, but 'more than half' no hold for paper vote, so we talk am carefully
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You put two results side by side and check which vote each statement fit.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Results different, so the votes no reliable and we no fit even say dodgeball get most
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Dodgeball get most both times. Wetin change na amount, no be order.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Paper vote probably make people worry less about wetin others think, so I trust paper result more and only say 'dodgeball get most'
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You decide which result to trust more based on difference in methods, and narrow wetin you talk.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Dem talk say only 4 students change mind between the two times. 2 change from dodgeball to board games, 2 change from dodgeball to skipping rope, and other 20 choose same thing both times.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: If this story true, which thought make sense?
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.after: For dodgeball 10 to pass 12, dem need add 3 or more of the 4 wey change (2 go make 12, same as half). Fact wey confirmed na 'dodgeball get most both times'.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The only difference between two results come from 4 people wey change. Other 20 same, so the two results similar well well
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You work out where difference between two votes come from, using number of people.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 4 people change, so both results useless
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: 20 people stay same, so throw everything away because of difference of 4 too much.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If you put the 4 wey change back to dodgeball, e go be 14, so first-day result na their real feeling
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You no fit know whether the 4 raise hand because dem fear others or change mind in one day. No reason dey to decide first day na the real answer.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Dodgeball get most both times, and whether e pass half (12) depend on feelings of the 4 wey change
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You find say how many of the 4 wey change join dodgeball 10 go decide the 12 standard.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.reflect: At first, you think say you fit talk anything? How paper result and story about 4 wey change their minds change the range of wetin you talk? Why phrase 'for this vote' dey needed?
z-m-11-04.s.s2.prompt: Write one or two sentences for class newspaper to report result of choosing game. Include which vote method dem use and the numbers, and write am so person fit see how far you fit claim.
z-m-11-04.s.s2.hint.0: Decide which vote numbers to write, and first state which method that vote use.
z-m-11-04.s.s2.hint.1: Split two votes into the parts where results same and where dem different, and state only same parts with confidence.
z-m-11-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: For your sentence, you tell fact (numbers from vote) apart from guess (real feelings)?
z-m-11-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Your answer show which of two methods' results you use as evidence, and why?
z-m-11-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You adjust the range of your statement without absolute words like 'everybody' or 'definitely'?
z-m-11-04.s.s2.model.0: For hand-raise vote, dodgeball get 14 out of 24, but for unnamed paper vote, results na dodgeball 10, board games 8 and skipping rope 6. Dodgeball get most both times, but whether e pass half depend on method, so e hard to talk surely.
z-m-11-04.s.s2.model.1: For secret paper vote, where people worry less about others watching, dodgeball get small lead with 10, board games 8 and skipping rope 6. So next week we go play dodgeball, and the week after, board games.
z-m-11-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: E state the method and use only paper-vote result as evidence, reflecting say the difference no big.

z-m-11-08.thinking.1: Make some examples wey satisfy conditions
z-m-11-08.title: One day wey start and end same: fit we say nothing change?
z-m-11-08.topic: Read changes for middle of line graph when start and end same
z-m-11-08.goal: Make counterexample to show say even when start and end values same, e fit still change in middle.
z-m-11-08.material:
Dem measure playground temperature every 3 hours and show am for line graph. (No picture. Values for points be these.)

| Time | 9 a.m. | 12 noon | 3 p.m. | 6 p.m. |
| Temperature (℃) | 14 | 19 | 21 | 14 |

Minjun talk say, "Temperature for 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. na same, 14℃, so playground temperature no change that day."
z-m-11-08.thinking.2: Tell apart wetin you fit know and wetin you no fit know from graph
z-m-11-08.prereq.0: Read points and values for line graph (Grade 4 level)
z-m-11-08.prereq.1: Find difference between big and small number
z-m-11-08.s.s1.prompt: Wetin you fit talk from this graph about Minjun statement?
z-m-11-08.s.s1.hint.0: Read values for all four graph points in order and write dem down.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether same value as starting value also dey for middle.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.o.a: Start and end same, so temperature in between must stay same all di time
z-m-11-08.s.s1.r.a: You guess say middle go same just by checking start and end. Read values for middle points themselves.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.o.b: Both middle points higher than 14℃ must be measuring mistake
z-m-11-08.s.s1.r.b: You throw away di values because middle points different. No evidence say dem measure am wrong.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.o.c: Both middle points higher than 14℃, so you no fit say nothing change
z-m-11-08.s.s1.r.c: You judge by reading both middle points, no be only start and end.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.o.d: Dem measure am every 3 hours, so you no fit know temperature for any time
z-m-11-08.s.s1.r.d: You fit read values for times dem measure (9, 12, 3, 6) from graph. Saying you no fit know anything too much.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.explain: If you read all four graph points, dem be 14, 19, 21, 14℃. Even though start and end same, e rise reach 7℃ in middle and come down again, so statement 'nothing change' no correct.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 other days wey Minjun statement wrong. Write temperatures (℃, whole numbers) for 9 a.m., 12 noon, 3 p.m., and 6 p.m. as t1, t2, t3, t4 in order. (Conditions: temperatures for 9 and 6 same; difference between highest and lowest of four values na 5℃ or more; difference between two nearby measurements na 8℃ or less; all values dey from 0℃ to 35℃. If 12 noon and 3 p.m. temperature pair different, e count as different example.)
z-m-11-08.s.s2.hint.0: First choose same temperature value for 9 a.m. and 6 p.m.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.hint.1: Choose middle two time values higher (or lower) than starting value, and check say difference between highest and lowest na 5 or more.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.ok.c1: All temperatures na whole numbers from 0℃ to 35℃.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.fail.c1: All temperatures must be whole numbers from 0 to 35.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.ok.c2: Temperature for 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. same.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.fail.c2: Temperature at 9 a.m. (t1) and 6 p.m. (t4) must be same.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.ok.c3: Difference between highest and lowest values na 5℃ or more, so temperature change during di day.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.fail.c3: Difference between highest and lowest values less than 5℃, so na day wey almost no change.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.ok.c4: Difference between two measurements beside each other na 8℃ or less.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.fail.c4: Changing by more than 8℃ in 3 hours too sudden.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.explain: Days like (14, 19, 21, 14), where start and end same but middle rise, or (20, 13, 12, 20), wey fall then rise again, fit happen. (14, 14, 14, 14) na day wey really no change, so e no be counterexample, and (10, 25, 25, 10) change by 15℃ in 3 hours, too sudden.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one example wey you make, and use numbers to write wetin you no fit know only from 'temperature for 9 and 6 same', but fit know by checking middle values.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: For di four values wey you make, cover start and end and think wetin you fit know from only di two middle values.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write side by side di statement you guess by looking only at start and end, and di statement you learn by checking all four points.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Di 'things you fit know' wey you mention really fit read from di four values you make?
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: For times wey dem no measure (for example, 10 a.m.), wetin you say you no know?
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: You separate whether you dey say 'start and end must not be same' or 'start and end alone no enough'?
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.model.0: My example na 14, 19, 21, 14℃. Even though 9 and 6 both 14℃, e be 19℃ at 12 and 21℃ at 3, so you fit tell temperature rise during di day then fall. If you only check start and end, you no go know this.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.model.1: Even if start and end same, middle values fit different. For my 12, 15, 17, 12, 9 and 6 both 12℃, but e rise to 17℃ at 3 p.m. But graph no tell me how e be at 10, between 9 and 12.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: E also talk say you no know times wey dem no measure.

z-m-11-03.title: Milk-carton bar graph: how much each scale mark?
z-m-11-03.topic: Choosing interval per mark on bar graph vertical axis
z-m-11-03.goal: Find different vertical-scale units making data land exactly on scale lines and fit paper; explain each easier to read differently.
z-m-11-03.material:
We wan show milk cartons collected by four Grade 4 groups in bar graph.
Group | Sun | Moon | Star | Forest
Cartons | 24 | 36 | 60 | 48
Graph paper rules:
- Vertical axis starts at 0. Each scale line means u cartons (natural number); there are n vertical marks.
- Paper allows n from 5 to 12.
- Biggest value (60) must fit, so top scale at least 60.
- Each bar end must land exactly on scale line for exact reading. 60. 4 24 36 60 48 0 5 12 60 60
z-m-11-03.thinking.0: Finding several designs that meet conditions
z-m-11-03.thinking.1: Finding problem in plan that breaks conditions
z-m-11-03.thinking.2: Compare advantages and disadvantages of designs
z-m-11-03.prereq.0: Read bar graph scale and draw bars (Grade 3 level)
z-m-11-03.prereq.1: Practice multiplication facts and division (Grades 3-4 level)
z-m-11-03.s.s1.prompt: Minho talk e go make each mark stand for 10 cartons and draw 6 vertical marks. (Top scale na 60.) Wetin problem dey with this plan?
z-m-11-03.s.s1.hint.0: Check the conditions for rules one by one against Minho plan (10, 6 marks).
z-m-11-03.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one whether 24, 36 and 48 dey on scale lines wey increase by 10.
z-m-11-03.s.s1.o.a: The longest bar (60) go outside paper and no fit inside graph
z-m-11-03.s.s1.r.a: 10×6=60, so 60 reach top scale exactly. You fit find out by checking plan with numbers.
z-m-11-03.s.s1.o.b: Scale no start from 0, so you no fit read values from bar heights
z-m-11-03.s.s1.r.b: This plan start from 0 too. Check plan against conditions in rules one by one.
z-m-11-03.s.s1.o.c: Only 6 vertical marks dey, so marks too few compared with the rules
z-m-11-03.s.s1.r.c: Rules only say number of marks must be 5 or more. 6 marks meet condition.
z-m-11-03.s.s1.o.d: Ends of 24, 36 and 48 bars dey between scale lines
z-m-11-03.s.s1.r.d: You find am correct. If scale na 10, 20, 30, ..., then 24 dey between 20 and 30.
z-m-11-03.s.s1.explain: 10×6=60, so e fit on paper and number of marks meet condition, but 24 dey between 20 and 30, 36 between 30 and 40, and 48 between 40 and 50. So dem no dey exactly on scale lines.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 scale plans wey meet all rules, with different scale sizes. (Number of cartons per mark u and number of vertical marks n. If scale size u different, count am as different plan.)
z-m-11-03.s.s2.hint.0: Decide size of one mark, then check whether 24, 36, 48 and 60 each dey exactly on scale lines wey go up by that size. If any value dey between scale lines, that size no go work.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.hint.1: If you find size wey all four values dey on scale lines, count how many marks you need to reach 60 and check say e meet condition for number of marks.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.ok.c1: u na natural number and n dey from 5 to 12.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.fail.c1: u must be natural number and n must dey from 5 to 12.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.ok.c2: Top scale na 60 or more, so 60 bar fit.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Top scale (u×n) less than 60, so longest bar go outside paper.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.ok.c3: Ends of all four bars dey exactly on scale lines.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.fail.c3: End of some bar dey between scale lines, so e hard to read value exactly.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.explain: With u=6, n=10, bar ends dey exactly at 4 marks, 6 marks, 10 marks and 8 marks. With u=12, n=5, dem be 2 marks, 3 marks, 5 marks and 4 marks. u=4 no work because you need more than 12 marks to reach 60, and u=3 or 2 no work because dem need more marks.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the two plans wey you make, and use numbers write wetin easy to read or drawback for this data. (For example, how the bar-height difference between groups look.)
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: For both plans, count how many marks of height difference dey between Sun group (24) and Moon group (36) bars.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare plan with plenty scale lines and plan with few, see which one make reading values easier.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. If one mark na ... cartons, ...
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You check again say scale and number of marks for your plan follow rules (60 fit, and values land exactly on scale lines)?
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: The advantage wey you mention na something you fit check with numbers, like bar-height difference?
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: You think about times wey the other plan fit better too?
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.model.0: I like plan where one mark stand for 6 cartons. Sun group na 4 marks and Moon group na 6 marks, so the difference na 2 marks, wey make am easy to compare by eye.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.model.1: If one mark na 12 cartons, only 5 marks dey, so graph fit on small paper and look neat. But Sun group (2 marks) and Moon group (3 marks) differ by only 1 mark, so difference look small.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: E mention both advantage and drawback.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.model.2: If one cell na 6, Sun group na 4 cells and Moon group na 6, so difference look like 2 cells and easy to read.

z-m-11-05.title: How many snack boxes we suppose prepare for book festival?
z-m-11-05.topic: Choose amount to prepare by looking past data (decision get different possible answers)
z-m-11-05.goal: Choose number of boxes using data from past five events as evidence, understand different answers fit conditions, then talk reason and risk of your own choice.
z-m-11-05.material:
For school book festival, each family member wey come get one snack. Number of people (people) wey come to past five events be: 

| Event | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th |
| People wey come | 32 | 41 | 36 | 44 | 38 |

One box get 6 snacks, and dem fit buy snacks only by box (you no fit buy singles). Each person get 1 snack. We still no know how many people go come next event.
z-m-11-05.thinking.0: Guess the range from biggest and smallest data values
z-m-11-05.thinking.1: Find different answers wey meet conditions
z-m-11-05.thinking.2: Talk about risk and benefit of a choice
z-m-11-05.prereq.0: Compare number sizes and find biggest and smallest numbers
z-m-11-05.prereq.1: Count total snacks wen you get several boxes of 6 (Grades 3-4 level)
z-m-11-05.s.s1.prompt: About how many people go come next event? Which statement make most sense from data of past five events?
z-m-11-05.s.s1.hint.0: First find smallest and biggest among five numbers.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.hint.1: Sort out whether each choice na 'something you fit really know from data' or 'something wey dem add but no dey data'.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.o.a: Past five events get between 32 and 44 people, so next one go be similar, but e fit fall outside that
z-m-11-05.s.s1.r.a: You guess based on range but leave open the chance say number fit outside.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.o.b: Most recent, 5th event, get 38 people, so 38 go come next time too because na latest number
z-m-11-05.s.s1.r.b: You take only last value. Look also say the five numbers different from each other.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.o.c: 44 na the most for past five, so e go hard for more than that to come next time
z-m-11-05.s.s1.r.c: You think say biggest value in past five na limit for future. New event fit get more.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.o.d: All five numbers different, so e seem hard to guess how many go come next
z-m-11-05.s.s1.r.d: Even if numbers different, clue dey say dem all between 32 and 44. To say you no fit guess at all throw away the data.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.explain: Data from five events no tell exact number for next event, but e show some range. Use that range, but think say e fit go outside too.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.prompt: Find 2 different box numbers wey meet all conditions and write them. (Conditions: enough even for day with most people in past five events, and leftover snacks no more than 10.)
z-m-11-05.s.s2.hint.0: Choose box number, find total snacks, and check whether e fall short or get leftovers wen 44 people come.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.hint.1: Find smallest number of boxes wey no fall short, then see whether buying one more box still leave no more than 10 extra.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.ok.c1: Number of boxes na natural number.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Number of boxes must be natural number of 1 or more.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.ok.c2: E no fall short even on the day with most people in past five events (44).
z-m-11-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Snacks fewer than 44, so e go fall short on day with most people in past five events.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.ok.c3: Wen 44 people come, leftover snacks no more than 10.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.fail.c3: Wen 44 people come, leftover snacks more than 10.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.explain: 8 boxes na 48 snacks, 4 remain; 9 boxes na 54, 10 remain. 7 boxes na 42, so on day 44 people come, 2 missing; 10 boxes na 60, 16 remain.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.prompt: If you really prepare, how many boxes you buy? You fit choose 7 boxes, no be only 8 or 9 above. Write number you choose and reason (risk of not enough, leftover amount) with numbers.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write total snacks for number of boxes you choose, then count how many of past five event days had more people than that number.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.hint.1: Think wetin happen wen snacks no reach and wen plenty remain, and say which one more troublesome.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. I go buy ... boxes because ...
z-m-11-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You calculate snack number for boxes you choose and compare with people numbers for past five events?
z-m-11-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You talk which one worry you more, risk of not enough or leftover amount?
z-m-11-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You think about possibility say more people fit come next time?
z-m-11-05.s.s3.model.0: I go buy 8 boxes (48 snacks). E enough even for 44 people, the most for past five events, and only 4 remain, so little waste.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.model.1: I go buy 9 boxes (54 snacks). This time more than 44 fit come, so I wan leave some room so snacks no go finish. If any remain, we fit use them next gathering.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.model.2: I think 7 boxes (42 snacks) okay too. Out of past five events, only the one time 44 people come go short by 2. If way dey to get few more snacks wen short, e better to reduce waste.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.modelNote.2: E break condition (no falling short), but e know the risk and even mention backup plan.

z-m-11-06.title: Same 20 students, different tables: who read am correctly?
z-m-11-06.topic: Choose intervals wen grouping data into intervals for table
z-m-11-06.goal: Check say even with same data, dividing intervals different fit change which interval get most; judge two claims wey read tables, and talk how to reduce misunderstanding.
z-m-11-06.material:
Number of books (books) wey 20 Grade 4 students read last month dey below. (Arranged from smallest to biggest.)

0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10

'3 to 5 books' include 3, 4 and 5 books. Jia make Table A, grouping by 3 books, and Minho make Table B, grouping by 4 books.

Table A (grouped by 3 books)
| Interval | 0 to 2 books | 3 to 5 books | 6 to 8 books | 9 to 11 books |
| Students (number) | 3 | 7 | 8 | 2 |

Table B (grouped by 4 books)
| Interval | 0 to 3 books | 4 to 7 books | 8 to 11 books |
| Students (number) | 8 | 5 | 7 |

Jia talk, 'Most students read 6 to 8 books,' and Minho talk, 'Most students read 0 to 3 books.'
z-m-11-06.thinking.0: Check both claims using same data
z-m-11-06.thinking.1: Find errors wey happen at interval borders
z-m-11-06.thinking.2: Reduce misunderstanding by changing how table dey made
z-m-11-06.prereq.0: Count data and arrange am for table (Grade 3-4 level)
z-m-11-06.prereq.1: Understand wetin interval like '0 to 2 books' mean when e include first and last numbers
z-m-11-06.s.s1.prompt: We check wetin each person talk against both tables and di 20 numbers above. Which judgment correct?
z-m-11-06.s.s1.hint.0: Add di number of students for each table and check say na 20.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.hint.1: For Table A and Table B, count di 20 numbers directly to check whether biggest box correct.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.o.a: Jia read di big box for Table A wrong, and Minho correct
z-m-11-06.s.s1.r.a: For Table A, 6 to 8 books na 8 students, di biggest box. Jia no read di table wrong.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.o.b: Both read their own table correct, and e look different because di intervals different
z-m-11-06.s.s1.r.b: You read di biggest box for both tables correctly, and see say how you divide intervals fit change di story.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.o.c: Both tables no look like dem count all 20 students, so both wrong
z-m-11-06.s.s1.r.c: Add up di number of students for each table. Both tables total 20.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.o.d: Minho read di big box for Table B wrong, and Jia correct
z-m-11-06.s.s1.r.d: For Table B, 0 to 3 books na 8 students, di biggest box. Minho no read di table wrong too.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.explain: For Table A, 6 to 8 books na di biggest, with 8 students; for Table B, 0 to 3 books na di biggest, with 8 students. Both tables total 20 students. Nobody read any table wrong; di 'interval wey get most' change based on how dem divide intervals.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.prompt: Seonyeong compare both tables and summarize am below. Which line strange? (Line numbers start from 1.)
z-m-11-06.s.s2.hint.0: From di 20 numbers, pick and write all di book numbers for students wey enter Table A 3 to 5 books box.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one whether all di numbers wey you pick fall inside Table B 4 to 7 books interval.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.line.0: 1. Table A get 3, 7, 8, and 2 students, and when you add dem all e give 20 students.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.line.1: 2. Table B get 8, 5, and 7 students, and when you add dem all e give 20 students.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.line.2: 3. Both tables count all 20 students, so only how dem group intervals different.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.line.3: 4. Table A 3 to 5 books box get 7 students, and all 7 enter Table B 4 to 7 books box, so Table B 4 to 7 box must get 7 or more.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.line.4: 5. For Table B, students wey read 3 books enter 0 to 3 books box, so Table B 0 to 3 books box look bigger than Table A.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.explain: Line 4 strange. Table A 3 to 5 books box include 5 students wey read 3 books, and 3 books go inside Table B 0 to 3 books box. So Table B 4 to 7 books box get 5 students, no be 7 or more. You miss say which box boundary value enter fit different for each table.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.prompt: You wan put 'books wey our class read in one month' for class newspaper as table. Write how you go decide di intervals and wetin you go show beside am to reduce misunderstanding.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.hint.0: First write one sentence about why Jia and Minho statements look different from each other.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.hint.1: To stop that from happening again, write one thing each wey newspaper reader suppose know and fit see.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., I would set the intervals ...
z-m-11-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Your method reduce cases where things look different, like Jia and Minho statements?
z-m-11-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You think of example like Table A and Table B and test your method with am?
z-m-11-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Apart from intervals, you think about showing di 20 numbers themselves too (like bar chart wey count each one)?
z-m-11-06.s.s3.model.0: I go write for di article how I divide intervals, and also show table wey use different intervals. If I print bar graph wey count books read one by one as 1 book, 2 books, ..., I think misunderstanding from intervals go reduce.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.model.1: If you group with only one kind interval, di story fit change, so I go check with two different interval sizes and only write statements wey come out same for both tables in newspaper.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: Na method to avoid deciding conclusion from one interval, and write only statements wey hold for both tables.

z-m-11-07.title: Remake book survey choices so dem no overlap
z-m-11-07.topic: Make survey options: no overlap and nothing left out
z-m-11-07.goal: Think how to read results when survey choices overlap or leave things out, then make choices yourself wey no overlap and allow everybody choose one.
z-m-11-07.material:
Class 3 for Grade 4 survey 'kind of book dem wan read' to buy new books for class library. Each person choose only one, and all 27 students answer. Survey choices and results be these.

| Choice | Fairy tale books | Comic books | Biographies | Story books | Science books |
| Students (number of people) | 8 | 9 | 3 | 5 | 2 |

(Survey say fairy tale books na books with imaginary stories, and story books na books with plot. History books and poetry books no dey among choices.)
z-m-11-07.thinking.1: Work out how overlap affect reading results
z-m-11-07.thinking.2: Make choices yourself and give reason
z-m-11-07.prereq.0: Read survey results arranged for table
z-m-11-07.prereq.1: Know difference between 'choose only one' and 'choose several'
z-m-11-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all problems wey fit come from choices for this survey.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.hint.0: Think one book wey fit both fairy tale books and story books. Which one you think student go choose?
z-m-11-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think few more kinds of books people wan read, and check whether any no fit anywhere among choices.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.o.a: There are 5 choices, so e hard for students to choose only one
z-m-11-07.s.s1.r.a: 5 no plenty. Problem no be number, na relationship between choices.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.o.b: Fairy tale books and story books overlap, so which box students choose fit differ from person to person
z-m-11-07.s.s1.r.b: You see say both choices similar, so people fit choose different ones for same book.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.o.c: Comic books dey among choices, so survey wrong
z-m-11-07.s.s1.r.c: Book being one of choices no make survey wrong. Think whether choices overlap or leave something out.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.o.d: Student wey wan read history books or poetry books no get choice to pick
z-m-11-07.s.s1.r.d: You find say some students wan read kind wey no dey survey. Dem answer, but dem no fit put their own thoughts.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.explain: If choices overlap, students with same idea fit enter different boxes, and if some kinds missing, dem students must force themselves choose closest box. Plenty choices or including one certain kind no be problem.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.prompt: Junho talk like this after seeing survey results. Which line strange? (Line numbers start from 1.)
z-m-11-07.s.s2.hint.0: Think whether among di 5 students wey choose story books, some fit also like fairy tale books.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.hint.1: For each line, check 'whether same student fit enter twice when you add or compare boxes'.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.line.0: 1. Each person choose only one, so 27, sum of all numbers for table, na number of students wey answer.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.line.1: 2. Comic books, with 9 students, na box wey most people choose.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.line.2: 3. Di 3 for biographies and 2 for science books na different students, so together dem na 5.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.line.3: 4. 8 students choose fairy tale books, so only 8 students like fairy tale books.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.line.4: 5. Students wey choose comic books na 1 more than students wey choose fairy tale books.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.explain: Line 4 strange. Among di 5 students wey choose story books, some fit also choose fairy tale books. Line 3 no show say choices no overlap; line 4 no prove only 8 students like fairy tale books. (Line numbers start from 1.)
z-m-11-07.s.s3.prompt: Remake survey choices. Write 5 or fewer options, make dem no overlap so each person fit choose exactly one.
z-m-11-07.s.s3.hint.0: First choose one way to divide books (for example, by content or shape), then write options.
z-m-11-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think of three book titles and check one by one whether each one enter exactly one of di choices.
z-m-11-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You test with examples whether any book fit two or more of your choices, or no fit any?
z-m-11-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Student wey wan read history books or poetry books get one option to choose?
z-m-11-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If you add box like 'other books', you think whether e fit become di biggest box?
z-m-11-07.s.s3.model.0: Choices: story books (including fairy tale books), comic books, science books, history and poetry books
z-m-11-07.s.s3.model.1: Choices: novels, comic books, knowledge books (science and history), poetry books, biographies
z-m-11-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: E divide books by content and check say dem no overlap, but no talk how to handle other books.
